A Release Plan is an evolving flowchart that describes what features will be delivered in upcoming releases. The Release Plan contains:

  • An ordered and estimated list of work to be done
  • Velocity estimates of the team and expected duration the team will be committed to working on the product
  • Definition of the Minimum Viable Product(s) (MVP)
  • Conditions of satisfaction (e.g. goals for schedule, scope and resources)

The Release Plan should clearly convey:

  • When the team will release
  • What components of the product will be released
  • To whom the released components will be delivered

There are three typical approaches that the Release Plan can take depending on the release strategy being employed:

  • Continuous delivery - the Release Plan will specify that developed components be released immediately once completed and signed off
  • Phased delivery - the Release Plan will specify that developed components be released at pre-determined dates which the team will work toward
  • Flexible delivery - the Release Plan will specify developed components be released once they are deemed sufficient by the team lead

Release Plans:

  • Can vary in size and duration
  • Are subject to change as the items contained in it evolve throughout the life of a project as new knowledge becomes available or changes to the scope of work occur, thereby impacting previously made assumptions
  • Should be revisited and updated on a regular basis, in Agile this would ideally occur after each sprint
  • With frequent releases shorten the feedback cycle which ultimately reduces the risk of building a product that does not meet stakeholders' expectations
  • May also include information on stakeholder demands, technology constraints and dependencies between work items
  • Do not need to include release dates when employing either a continuous or flexible delivery approach
To document release approach, dates and plan for delivering increments of a product.

Consequences of not producing this work product include:

  • Unable to inform the business about future releases and expected delivery dates
  • Unintentionally slip into a waterfall approach of design, develop, test and release
  • Ambiguity within the team with regard to release ambition and responsibilities
A Release Plan may not be as relevant for those projects that only have a few small increments to release.
